title: AWS Security, Identity and Access Management

questions.question: In the shared responsibility model, AWS is responsible for providing what?

explanation.summary: AWS is responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs AWS services.
explanation.why: Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, AWS manages the security of the cloud, including hardware, software, networking, and facilities that run AWS services.
keyPoints: AWS manages underlying hardware and networking
explanation.comparison: Customers are responsible for security in the cloud, while AWS handles security of the cloud.

explanation.summary: This phrase is not part of the AWS Shared Responsibility Model terminology.
explanation.why: AWS officially defines responsibilities as security of the cloud and security in the cloud. The phrase security to the cloud is not a recognized AWS concept.
explanation.confusion: The wording resembles AWS terminology but is not an official term.

explanation.summary: AWS does not use this phrase in its responsibility model.
explanation.why: AWS distinguishes between security of the cloud and security in the cloud. Security for the cloud is not an official responsibility category.

explanation.summary: Customers are responsible for protecting resources and data they place in AWS.
explanation.why: Security in the cloud refers to customer responsibilities such as IAM, operating systems, applications, and data protection.
explanation.keyDistinction: AWS secures infrastructure, while customers secure workloads and configurations.

questions.question: In the shared responsibility model, which of the following are examples of security in the cloud?

options.text: Compliance with compute security standards and regulations

explanation.summary: AWS manages compliance for the infrastructure layer.
explanation.why: AWS is responsible for maintaining compliance of the infrastructure that operates AWS services.

options.text: Physical security of the facilities in which the services operate

explanation.summary: AWS manages the physical protection of data centers and facilities.
explanation.why: Physical security is part of AWS responsibilities under security of the cloud.

explanation.summary: Customers configure network access controls for their resources.
explanation.why: Security groups are customer-managed firewall rules that control inbound and outbound traffic to AWS resources.

options.text: Encryption of data at rest and data in transit

explanation.summary: Customers are responsible for protecting their application data.
explanation.why: Customers decide whether and how to encrypt their data using AWS encryption services and configurations.

explanation.summary: AWS protects the infrastructure that supports cloud services globally.
explanation.why: Protection of AWS Regions, Availability Zones, and networking infrastructure is handled by AWS.

questions.question: Which of the following is the responsibility of AWS under the AWS shared responsibility model?

explanation.summary: Customers manage application configuration in AWS environments.
explanation.why: Configuration of applications deployed in AWS remains the customer's responsibility.

explanation.summary: AWS maintains the hardware infrastructure supporting cloud services.
explanation.why: AWS manages servers, networking equipment, storage devices, and facilities used to provide cloud services.
keyPoints: Customers do not manage physical servers

explanation.summary: Customers control access management and data security.
explanation.why: IAM permissions, application authentication, and data protection are customer responsibilities.

explanation.summary: Customers are responsible for maintaining their AMIs.
explanation.why: Custom AMIs include customer-defined software and operating systems, which customers must patch and manage.

questions.question: When creating an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy, what are the two types of access that can be granted to a user?

explanation.summary: Institutional access is not an AWS IAM access type.
explanation.why: AWS IAM defines access types as programmatic access and AWS Management Console access.

explanation.summary: Authorized access is a generic security term rather than an IAM access type.
explanation.why: AWS IAM does not classify access using this terminology.

explanation.summary: Programmatic access enables API and CLI interaction with AWS services.
explanation.why: Programmatic access uses access keys for SDKs, CLI tools, and API requests.

explanation.summary: Console access enables users to log in through the AWS web interface.
explanation.why: IAM users can authenticate using usernames and passwords to access the AWS Management Console.

explanation.summary: Root access refers to the AWS account root user rather than IAM access types.
explanation.why: The root user is separate from IAM users and should be used only for limited account-level tasks.

questions.question: True or False? AWS Organizations enables you to consolidate multiple AWS accounts so that you centrally manage them.

explanation.summary: AWS Organizations centrally manages multiple AWS accounts.
explanation.why: AWS Organizations provides consolidated billing, centralized governance, and policy management for multiple AWS accounts.

explanation.summary: AWS Organizations is specifically designed for centralized account management.
explanation.why: The service exists to organize and manage multiple AWS accounts from a single location.

questions.question: Which of the following are best practices to secure your account using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)?

options.text: Provide users with default administrative privileges.

explanation.summary: Administrative privileges should follow least privilege principles.
explanation.why: AWS recommends granting only permissions required to perform specific tasks.

options.text: Leave unused and unnecessary users and credentials in place.

explanation.summary: Unused accounts and credentials increase security risk.
explanation.why: AWS recommends removing unused credentials and accounts to reduce attack surfaces.
explanation.performanceImpact: Unused credentials can become security vulnerabilities.

explanation.summary: IAM helps centrally control access to AWS services and resources.
explanation.why: IAM enables administrators to define who can access resources and what actions they can perform.

options.text: Avoid using IAM groups to grant the same access permissions to multiple users.

explanation.summary: IAM groups simplify permission management for multiple users.
explanation.why: AWS recommends using groups to efficiently assign permissions to multiple users with similar responsibilities.

explanation.summary: Fine-grained permissions help enforce least privilege access.
explanation.why: Granular IAM policies reduce unnecessary access and improve account security.

questions.question: Which of the following should be done by the AWS account root user?

explanation.summary: Application access management is typically handled through IAM roles and policies.
explanation.why: AWS recommends avoiding daily operational use of the root account.

explanation.summary: Service integrations are usually configured using IAM roles and permissions.
explanation.why: The root user should only perform restricted account-level actions.

explanation.summary: Granular permissions are commonly managed through IAM administrators.
explanation.why: AWS recommends using IAM users with administrative privileges instead of the root account for routine administration.

explanation.summary: Certain account-level operations require root user privileges.
explanation.why: Changing the AWS support plan is one of the tasks reserved for the AWS account root user.
explanation.keyDistinction: Root-only tasks include billing and account-level configuration changes.

questions.question: After initial login, what does AWS recommend as the best practice for the AWS account root user?

options.text: Delete the AWS account root user

explanation.summary: The root user is permanently associated with the AWS account.
explanation.why: AWS accounts always contain a root user and it cannot be deleted.

options.text: Revoke all permissions on the AWS account root user

explanation.summary: The root user inherently has full account permissions.
explanation.why: Permissions cannot be revoked from the root user account.

options.text: Restrict permission on the AWS account root user

explanation.summary: Root user permissions cannot be restricted through IAM policies.
explanation.why: The root account always has unrestricted access to AWS services and resources.

options.text: Delete the access keys of the AWS account root user

explanation.summary: AWS recommends removing unnecessary root access keys for security.
explanation.why: Root access keys provide unrestricted API access and should be deleted unless absolutely required.

True or False? AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) enables you to assess, audit, and evaluate the configurations of your AWS resources.

explanation.summary: AWS KMS manages encryption keys rather than resource configuration auditing.
explanation.why: AWS KMS is used for creating and managing cryptographic keys for encryption operations.

explanation.summary: AWS Config assesses and audits resource configurations rather than AWS KMS.
explanation.why: AWS Config evaluates resource configurations and compliance, while AWS KMS focuses on encryption key management.
explanation.comparison: AWS Config handles auditing and compliance, whereas AWS KMS handles encryption.
